newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin spends Russian Christmas in bed with cold.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin spends Russian Christmas in bed with cold.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin had to spend part of Russia's Orthodox Christmas Day in bed on Tuesday after coming down with a heavy cold, but the Kremlin inisted his illness had nothing to do with his recent heart surgery.
Doctors advised the 65-year-old leader to take it easy at his country residence outside Moscow after he went sick on Monday and cancelled his engagements for the next few days.
"The president will spend today at his residence at Gorky-9, most probably with his family," a Kremlin spokesman told Reuters. "He will be partially confined to bed."

Yeltsin, who looked tired and wan in television clips of his meeting with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Saturday, was following an "intensive course of treatment" but did not have a particularly high temperature.
The spokesman had no more details of his illness or medicine but added his doctors saw no need for Yeltsin to visit hospital.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted unnamed sources as saying he was a victim of a cold epidemic that has swept Moscow over the New Year holidays, hitting the presidential family.
Yeltsin's younger grandson Gleb fell ill on New Year's Eve and the president's wife, Naina, had later had to take to her bed with a fever, Tass said.

Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Monday the president had a heavy cold and a temperature of 37.5 degrees Celsius (99.5 Fahrenheit) but stressed the illness had no relation to his heart bypass operation on November 5.

Veteran Texan heart surgeon Michael DeBakey, who advised on the operation, told Reuters in Houston late on Monday that Yeltsin's heart was all but back to normal and a should not pose any special problems.

"Based on the reports I'm getting, it would appear his cardiac function has been virtually restored to normal," DeBakey said. Yeltsin's recovery was "right on schedule" and the surgery would not leave him susceptible to infections such as a cold.
"It should make him more resistant," DeBakey said.
He added the cold was "transient and self-limited" but doctors would keep an eye on it. "Any cold should be taken seriously because it can develop into other things," he said.

DeBakey said he did not think the president's return to work at the end of last month had contributed to his catching cold. "He promised me he would be a good patient and I think he has been," said DeBakey, 88.
Yeltsin declared January 7 -- Christmas Day according to the old Orthodox calendar -- a public holiday in 1992 after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

He has encouraged the resurrection of the state Orthodox Church, which was controlled and repressed but not dismantled under atheistic communism, and has exploited its tradition and influence to bolster the legitimacy of his own position.

Patriarch Alexiy II, the head of the church, however chided the Kremlin in a Christmas Eve statement for its failure to meet promises to pay unpaid wages and pensions before officiating at a packed midnight service in Moscow's ornate Epiphany church.
Some data suggest up to half Russia's 150 million people are active Orthodox believers despite years of official atheism.
